title: Do Existing Legal Ethics Rules Cover AI? — full episode transcript
pub: Talk Justice, Legal Services Corporation / Legal Talk Network
author: Andrew Perlman

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Perlman does not address the cluster’s concern that automating junior work may disrupt apprenticeship and expertise reproduction. He instead reframes AI and training as an access-to-justice investment that could expand legal-aid capacity with existing resources, provided lawyers receive proper training and suitable tools.
qs: But I believe that if you put these tools in the hands of lawyers, again, properly trained with the right tools, they are going to be able to help a lot more people with the same resources.

So I do think that the ROI of investing in generative AI and generative AI training may present an opportunity for legal aid offices that’s unlike any other technological investments that may have been available in the past.

st.t: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s access-to-justice framing by linking AI experimentation to serving more people amid severe unmet civil legal need. Its emphasis on learning both capabilities and limits through hands-on use is consistent with cautious implementation, although it provides no evidence that AI has reduced unmet need or concrete safeguards for client-facing deployment.
qs: So I’m seeing folks across the country in legal aid offices just really curious about how we can be leveraging this technology to serve more people.
Use it for in your daily life so that you get a feel for what it can do, and just as importantly, what it can’t do.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that existing professional duties and sanctions govern fabricated filings rather than AI use itself. It specifically endorses the technology-neutral side of the cluster’s acknowledged disclosure dispute, arguing that routine AI-use disclosure is unnecessary and difficult to define as AI becomes embedded in ordinary software.
qs: And the reason it’s not necessary is that we have existing rules that would prevent lawyers from filing a brief with fictitious citations in it that’s longstanding as a basis for discipline or a violation of Rule 11.

But the idea of having lawyers disclose to the court every time they’ve used a generative AI tool is wholly unnecessary and also potentially problematic as these tools evolve and the lines between generative AI and just traditional professional software, those lines are blurring.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s practical agenda of supported, preparatory experimentation by encouraging early learning and groundwork before legal deployment. It does not claim that this activity has improved access to justice or legal outcomes, so it remains consistent with the synthesis’s distinction between adoption activity and proven access gains.
qs: In the meantime, I hope that those who work in those kinds of settings will at least on their own, discover the potential so that when the time comes to roll it out in a law related setting, they’re ready.
Yeah, we can be laying the groundwork now.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s view that generative AI may expand access to legal help but requires advance preparation and purposeful implementation. Its claims are prospective and preparatory rather than empirical: it forecasts major impact and encourages readiness without demonstrating improved access or service outcomes.
qs: In the meantime, I hope that those who work in those kinds of settings will at least on their own, discover the potential so that when the time comes to roll it out in a law related setting, they’re ready.
His current research focuses on the ethical use of technology like generative AI in legal practice, including the potential impact of gen AI to increase access to legal help.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI could expand meaningful legal help while treating gains as conditional rather than automatic. It predicts greater legal-aid capacity with appropriate tools, deployment and training, but acknowledges resource constraints and offers no measured evidence that uptake has produced sustained justice-gap reductions.
qs: What I think might be a little bit different about this technology is the potential for scaling and how many more people legal aid office can help if these technologies are appropriately developed and deployed.
There’s always been resource constraints on the ability to invest in new technology, in especially legal aid offices and the like.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports bounded, practice-led AI adoption by urging lawyers to experiment with everyday uses, learn both capabilities and limitations, and persist through poor initial outputs. It also frames adoption against unmet legal need, without claiming that AI alone closes the justice gap or providing evidence on productivity, verification costs, or staffing effects.
qs: Use it for in your daily life so that you get a feel for what it can do, and just as importantly, what it can’t do.
When I talk to people, I hear, I tried it, it gave me garbage or it didn’t give me a good answer, or it gave me the wrong answer, or I could have done better.

st.t: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s case for hands-on, selective experimentation rather than unqualified reliance. It urges lawyers to learn AI capabilities through use while stressing that legal applications must respect organisational rules and confidentiality constraints; it offers practical guidance, not evidence of reliable performance or net productivity gains.
qs: And so as a practical matter, I can’t recommend more strongly that every lawyer out there in every setting just start using the tools.

So when it starts to get to law related use cases, it gets tricky in a hurry for a variety of reasons, depending on the setting, depending on what constraints your organization has and rules already in place about the use of the tools.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s technology-neutral, human-accountability framework: existing duties of competence, confidentiality and supervision govern generative AI, lawyers must monitor the technology as it evolves, and false or fictitious court submissions remain the lawyer’s responsibility. It also aligns with the cluster’s opposition to blanket AI-use disclosure, though it does not address whether verification costs consume efficiency gains in depth.
qs: So I think the big takeaway here is, and I think the ethics opinions reflect this point, is that we just need to look at the existing rules, understand how they play out in this context, and that provides pretty good guidance for lawyers when they’re thinking about what they need to do with regard to generative ai.

Now, it may be useful to remind lawyers that these tools make mistakes and that if they file a brief or any document with the court that has fictitious information, citations that they can and will be disciplined for that.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the proposition that generative AI will become integrated into lawyers’ work and displace established task workflows while lawyers remain responsible practitioners. Its claims are long-range predictions, however, and provide no direct evidence about staffing, employment or business-model outcomes.
qs: But I think if we fast forward 25 years from now, anyone who is not using these tools, you would have to wonder about their competence.
How are you just creating every document by opening up word processor or whatever it will be at that time to a blank screen and starting to type?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source broadly supports selective, human-centred deployment: it treats impact as varying by task and practice area, conditions gains on appropriate tools, training and deployment, and favours existing professional duties plus practical guardrails. Its claims about transformative impact and legal-aid scaling are predictions rather than evidence of general competence or realised outcomes, but they do not displace its cautious, context-specific position.
qs: I think there are some areas of practice and some types of tasks where lawyers have been too slow to adapt to technology, but in other circumstances that’s not necessarily the case.
But I believe that if you put these tools in the hands of lawyers, again, properly trained with the right tools, they are going to be able to help a lot more people with the same resources.

kp.k: Existing professional rules largely accommodate generative AI
kp.d: Perlman argues that existing confidentiality, competence and supervision obligations provide useful guidance for generative AI, a position he says appears in almost all ethics opinions he has read. He attributes this adaptability to deliberately technology-neutral updates proposed by the ABA Ethics 2020 Commission about 15 years earlier. This is his interpretation of the regulatory framework, not a claim that new AI-specific rules have been adopted.
qs: I think one theme that I have seen in almost all of the opinions I’ve read to date is that the existing rules of professional conduct are doing their job when it comes to generative ai.
we did not propose changes that were intended to respond to very specific technical developments at that time.

you look at issues like the duty of confidentiality or the duty to supervise non-lawyer assistance in Rule 5.3 or Rule 1.1, the duty of competence, all of those concepts apply pretty well to generative ai.

kp.k: Competence may eventually require generative AI use
kp.d: Perlman predicts that, in 25 years, nonuse of generative AI could call lawyers’ competence into question, particularly if they still draft every document from a blank screen. His analogy is email’s transition from confidentiality concern to licensing requirement in some bars. He does not assert a present universal duty to use AI: he stresses that technology obligations depend on technology and practice context, and recommends monitoring AI’s evolution.
qs: So we went from a bar association saying, be careful about the use of this technology to now you can’t even be licensed unless you have an email address.
But I think if we fast forward 25 years from now, anyone who is not using these tools, you would have to wonder about their competence.
when it comes to the duty of competence, lawyers need to pay attention to generative AI as it evolves in the coming years.

kp.k: Transformative effects are predicted over a longer horizon
kp.d: Perlman predicts that generative AI will affect legal work more profoundly than email, digital research or e-discovery. Drawing on his own regular experimentation and a change-timing observation he attributes to Bill Gates, he expects truly transformative changes closer to 10 years than two years. He describes this as a reason for preparation and excitement rather than an immediate crisis; no measured productivity or adoption findings are supplied.
qs: I believe that this will be the most important technology ever invented for the legal profession.
And that includes email, electronic research, digital research, e-discovery. All of those are important, but I think generative AI will be the most important of them all.
I tend to think that the truly transformative changes will be beyond two years, it’ll be closer to 10, but they’re coming.

kp.k: Regulators should avoid premature technology-specific restrictions
kp.d: Perlman recommends examining existing laws and rules before introducing new regulation, arguing that excessive caution could harm clients and organizations’ future health. He acknowledges serious AI risks and risks from inaction, but urges regulatory humility. Moon separately supplies a historical anecdote: Tennessee issued restrictive email guidance in 1998 and reversed its position before that year ended.
qs: I don’t want to see us be too quick to say, you can’t use it, you shouldn’t use it.
Now, of course, there are risks from doing nothing. I don’t want to understate that because there are some serious risks associated with AI in general, in generative AI in particular.
So don’t try to regulate in a one-off way, try to understand what’s already out there before going in a new direction.
1998 before the end of that same year, they issued an opinion saying the opposite.

kp.k: Court bans and disclosure orders are often unnecessary
kp.d: Perlman criticizes broad court AI bans and mandatory generative-AI-use disclosures as unnecessary or overbroad. He argues that existing disciplinary rules and Rule 11 already address fabricated citations, while reminders about mistakes and sanctions could suffice. He also identifies an implementation problem: generative autocomplete is increasingly embedded in ordinary software, potentially making routine sentence completion disclosure-triggering under some orders. The courts and orders discussed are not identified.
qs: we have existing rules that would prevent lawyers from filing a brief with fictitious citations in it that’s longstanding as a basis for discipline or a violation of Rule 11.

Now, it may be useful to remind lawyers that these tools make mistakes and that if they file a brief or any document with the court that has fictitious information, citations that they can and will be disciplined for that.
the lines between generative AI and just traditional professional software, those lines are blurring.
the judicial standing orders for the most part are unnecessary and in many cases unwise.

kp.k: Interpretive ethics guidance can facilitate responsible adoption
kp.d: Perlman distinguishes restrictive judicial orders from bar ethics opinions explaining how existing obligations apply. He regards attention to AI as understandable because of its transformative potential and publicized fabricated-citation incidents, and argues that clear ethical guardrails can help lawyers adopt tools rather than leave them guessing about permissibility.
qs: some of the famous or infamous examples that were in the press of lawyers putting fictitious citations into briefs using generative AI capture the public’s attention and the profession’s attention
I think by doing so, it will help lawyers adopt these tools more readily than if there were no ethics opinions at all.
here are the guardrails, here is what you can do, here’s what you should be careful about.

kp.k: Lawyers should learn through repeated low-stakes experimentation
kp.d: Perlman recommends beginning with any useful task, including personal information seeking or rewording a press release, rather than treating generative AI solely as a legal research tool. He advises persistence after poor results, learning how prompts affect output and comparing tools. These recommendations concern practical familiarity with capabilities and limitations; his favorable assessment of current free models is experiential rather than a benchmark result.
qs: Use it for in your daily life so that you get a feel for what it can do, and just as importantly, what it can’t do.
And a second piece of advice, don’t give up quickly.
usually people don’t know much about the concept of prompt engineering and how different the output is depending on how you ask the question.
there are many different tools out there, and you might get a different response depending on which tool you use as well.

kp.k: Public documents offer an entry into legal experimentation
kp.d: Perlman cautions that legal applications quickly raise setting-specific constraints and organizational rules. He suggests experimenting without confidential information, including anonymization or asking AI to critique an opponent’s publicly filed brief and identify weaknesses or counterarguments. He reports increasingly capable custom GPT projects and anticipates a substantial shift in generating legal information and documents, without supplying measured accuracy results.
qs: when it starts to get to law related use cases, it gets tricky in a hurry for a variety of reasons, depending on the setting, depending on what constraints your organization has and rules already in place about the use of the tools.
You can anonymize information and still get a sense of what it can do.

You get a brief from an opponent, it’s public information, it’s filed with the court, take it, upload it to your favorite generative AI tool, ask it to analyze it, tell me the weaknesses. What are some arguments against this position?
we’re in the early stages of a pretty massive shift in how we generate information and legal documents.

kp.k: Public self-help should be weighed against unmet legal need
kp.d: Moon reports that the latest LSC survey found 92% of legal problems experienced by low-income Americans received no meaningful help; she calls this a justice failure rate. Perlman uses that reported baseline to argue for considering appropriately structured public-facing AI self-help, including document generation, rather than focusing only on risks. He acknowledges enormous peril as well as potential; the discussion offers no demonstrated self-help outcomes or additional survey details.
qs: the latest LSC survey revealed that 92% of the legal problems experienced by low-income Americans get no meaningful help.
Of course, enormous peril as well, but enormous potential.
we always have to ask the question relative to what you mentioned, that 92% figure relative to that, how is that worse?
And if these tools when appropriately structured and made available to the public can enable folks to help themselves, we absolutely need to consider that possibility.

kp.k: Legal aid scaling depends on tools and training
kp.d: Responding to Moon’s concern about constrained legal aid budgets, Perlman predicts that properly developed and deployed AI, paired with lawyer training, could enable offices to serve substantially more people with the same resources. He suggests the return on AI and training investment may exceed that of earlier technology investments, but frames this as cautious optimism and acknowledges broad adoption may remain some time away. He encourages staff to build familiarity in advance; no quantified return or service-volume evidence is offered.
qs: But I believe that if you put these tools in the hands of lawyers, again, properly trained with the right tools, they are going to be able to help a lot more people with the same resources.

the ROI of investing in generative AI and generative AI training may present an opportunity for legal aid offices that’s unlike any other technological investments that may have been available in the past.

I’m cautiously optimistic that we will eventually reach the point where it becomes so obvious that that is a worthwhile investment that we’ll see it happen across the board, but I think that we may be some time away from reaching that moment.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Andrew Perlman predicts that generative AI will have a greater impact on lawyers’ work than any previous legal technology.
pts.d: Perlman explicitly ranks its expected significance above email, electronic legal research and e-discovery. He anticipates a substantial shift in generating information and legal documents, rather than merely another incremental software improvement. These are predictions grounded in his experience using the tools, not reported measurements of profession-wide change.

pts.k: Perlman predicts that using generative AI will eventually become an expectation of competent legal practice.
pts.d: He anticipates a transition from present confidentiality concerns to questioning the competence of lawyers who do not use the tools. He illustrates this through document drafting: beginning every document from a blank screen would become difficult to justify. This is a future competence prediction, not a statement that all lawyers already have an unconditional obligation to use generative AI.

pts.k: Perlman argues that existing professional-conduct rules already provide a workable framework for generative AI and that explanatory ethics opinions can facilitate adoption.
pts.d: He identifies confidentiality, Rule 5.3 on supervising nonlawyer assistance and Rule 1.1 on competence as applicable concepts. Rather than proposing a new AI-specific regime, he argues that explaining existing guardrails reduces lawyers’ uncertainty and helps them adopt the tools. He distinguishes this supportive guidance from restrictive judicial orders.

pts.k: Perlman argues that AI-specific bans and blanket court-disclosure requirements can unnecessarily restrict useful technology and become problematic as AI is integrated into ordinary software.
pts.d: He considers many judicial standing orders unnecessary because existing obligations already prohibit fictitious filings. He predicts practical difficulties as the boundary between generative AI and conventional professional software blurs, citing sentence completion in Word, Outlook and Gmail. He warns that premature restrictions can harm clients and organizations, while expressly acknowledging the risks of regulatory inaction.

pts.k: Perlman identifies document critique and argument development as practical lawyer-assistance uses, with output dependent on prompting and tool choice.
pts.d: He proposes experimenting with an opponent’s publicly filed brief to identify weaknesses and counterarguments. This is a suggested augmentation use case, not evidence that the output can be relied on without checking. He argues that an initially poor answer should not be treated as conclusive about capability because question formulation and the selected tool affect the response.

pts.k: Perlman predicts that properly deployed generative AI could enable legal aid offices to help substantially more people with the same resources.
pts.d: He distinguishes this potential capacity gain from conventional technology expenditure and suggests that investment in AI and training could offer unusually strong returns for legal aid. He provides no quantified gain, implementation cost or observed legal-aid outcome. His position is cautiously optimistic and conditional on suitable tools, training and deployment.

pts.k: Perlman sees substantial potential for public-facing AI legal self-help, alongside substantial risks.
pts.d: He extends his argument beyond lawyer assistance to people generating legal documents and helping themselves. He argues that the relevant comparison includes receiving no meaningful legal help, not only receiving lawyer-delivered service. He conditionally endorses considering appropriately structured public tools, without claiming that unsupervised legal AI has already been shown safe or effective.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Perlman supports his transformation and competence predictions with personal experimentation and an analogy to email adoption.
pts.d: He reports using generative AI almost daily, building custom GPTs and observing improving capabilities in law-related projects. His historical analogy is that bars initially warned about email confidentiality but later required email addresses. The transcript supplies no controlled productivity study or benchmark establishing his predictions.

pts.k: His regulatory claims draw on professional experience, his reading of ethics opinions and existing rules governing false court filings.
pts.d: Perlman invokes his role as chief reporter of the ABA Ethics 2020 Commission and its deliberate effort to make technology-related amendments durable. He reports a common theme in opinions he has read, rather than presenting a systematic survey. For court filings, he points to longstanding disciplinary rules and Rule 11 as already addressing fictitious citations. His examples of misuse and court restrictions are not named cases or measured hallucination rates.

pts.k: The access-to-justice argument uses unmet legal need as context, rather than evidence of demonstrated AI outcomes.
pts.d: Perlman explicitly takes up the 92% figure introduced by the interviewer as an LSC survey finding about low-income Americans’ legal problems receiving no meaningful help. It is not presented as his own research or as a measured AI effect. His scaling and self-help claims remain prospective; the transcript offers no trial demonstrating increased legal-aid capacity or improved outcomes for unrepresented users.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Perlman expects truly transformative effects closer to ten years than two years after the 2024 interview.
pts.d: He distinguishes effects already beginning to appear from a later transformation. He cautions against treating adaptation as an immediate crisis, while maintaining that substantial change is coming. His timeframe is an expectation, not a dated implementation forecast.

pts.k: Present-day experimentation is qualified by confidentiality, organizational constraints and the need to learn capabilities and limitations.
pts.d: Perlman recommends starting immediately, including with personal or nonlegal tasks. For legal work, he emphasizes that appropriate uses depend on the setting and organizational rules. He suggests anonymized information or public documents as ways to explore capabilities without disclosing confidences. He does not characterize every tool as suitable for every practice.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern practicing lawyers, legal aid organizations and clients, courts and regulators, and people without legal help.
pts.d: Lawyers face changing drafting practices, learning requirements and eventual competence expectations. Legal aid offices may expand service capacity despite limited budgets, provided they obtain suitable tools and training. Clients and organizations may lose benefits if regulation is prematurely restrictive. Courts retain responsibility for enforcing reliable filings as AI becomes embedded in everyday software. Members of the public could gain self-help options but also face risks from misuse and erroneous output. Perlman does not provide concrete forecasts of staffing reductions, pricing changes or market-share shifts.
